resources.string:
BentoBar draws your items (network speed, timer, calendar, tools…) on the status bar. Android allows that only through an accessibility service.

With it on, BentoBar: reads the status bar's layout, to find free space for your items; with the App menu bar on (Look), reads which app is in front (its package name) and the system's title bar over its window, to show that app's menus and press its title bar's buttons from the Window menu, and, when you start a quick action that only the launcher may start, the menu of that app's taskbar icon; reads the colour of the status bar clock, so your items match it; and runs the system actions you pick in the Tools menu or as a Shortcut item, such as screenshot or lock.

It never reads what other apps show inside their windows, and doesn't watch your keyboard, mouse or touches. Nothing the service reads ever leaves your Googlebook: BentoBar never collects or shares it.

BentoBar goes online for three items only, and only after you set them up: Weather asks Open-Meteo about the city you search for (or, with My location, about where the device is, rounded to about 10 km), Flight asks AirLabs about the flight you enter, and US stocks asks Finnhub about the stocks you follow, the last two with a key of your own. BentoBar sends nothing else anywhere: not your layout, your calendar, what\'s playing or anything it measures. It has no accounts of its own, no ads and no analytics, and it sends its developer nothing. Its accessibility service reads the status bar (its layout and its clock\'s colour) and, with the App menu bar on, which app is in front and the system\'s title bar over its window, never what apps show inside their windows. With Usage access on, it also reads how much data and storage each app uses, for the Network and Storage menus, and nothing else.

Weather sends Open-Meteo the city you search for. For the forecast it sends the coordinates of the city you pick, rounded to about a kilometre: about every 30 minutes while the bar is on screen, and when you open its menu or press Refresh. With My location it sends where this device is instead, rounded to about 10 km: BentoBar asks Android for the approximate location only while such an item is in the bar or waits in Hidden to show for rain or snow, or while BentoBar\'s settings window is open, and keeps it and its forecast in memory only. Open-Meteo sees your IP address, as any website does, and may keep it in its logs for 90 days.
